findings.situation: A filer who lived all of 2025 in Albany or Buffalo (outside New York City) truthfully answers No to the city question, so the State question is never asked and the line is set to false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30, Resident: "You are a New York State resident for income tax purposes if: • You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more in New York State ... • Your domicile is New York State."
findings.why: The line's own description says it is the State question asked only after a No to the city question. The gate does the opposite: it asks it only after a Yes. Inside that branch, a city resident gets "No", so the State residency answer can never reach the filers it is meant for.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer lived in New York City all year but the spouse did not. The filer answers Yes for themselves, and the residency status that matters for the spouse is never determined.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, New York City and Yonkers: "see the definitions of a New York State resident, nonresident, and part-year resident above, and substitute New York City or Yonkers in place of New York State."
findings.why: The gate question asks only about "you". The gated helper asks about "you (and your spouse, on a joint return)", so the gate does not cover the spouse.

findings.situation: A person domiciled outside New York City keeps a permanent place of abode in the city for substantially all of the year and spends 184 or more days there. That person is a city resident under the cited test, but may truthfully say they did not 'live in' the city all year.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more ... whether or not you were domiciled in New York State"; p. 31: "substitute New York City ... in place of New York State"
findings.why: The cited text defines residence by domicile, or by a permanent place of abode plus 184 days. The gate instead asks whether the filer 'lived in' the city all year, which is a different condition.

findings.situation: A New York City domiciliary spent most of 2025 on a temporary work assignment elsewhere and does not count it as 'time away' while their 'home stayed in the city'. Such a filer could reasonably answer No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30, Domicile: "If you move to a new location but intend to stay there only for a limited amount of time (no matter how long), your domicile does not change."
findings.why: 'Did you live in New York City' reads as physical presence. The help text's reference to time away does not clearly tell a filer on a long-term relocation that domicile governs.

findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: "Report your sales or use tax liability on this line. You owe sales or compensating use tax if you: • purchased an item or service subject to tax that is delivered to you in New York State without payment of New York State and local tax to the seller"
findings.why: The gate question asks only whether "you" bought something, with no mention of a spouse. A filer can answer no when the spouse's purchases create the liability that the part-year abode proration applies to. findings.situation: A filer paid New York tax at a lower local rate in one county, then used the item in their home county, which has a higher rate and is outside New York City.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: "You may also owe an additional local tax if you use property or services in another locality in New York State, other than the locality to which you paid tax. You owe use tax to the second locality if you were a resident of that locality at the time of the purchase, and its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid."
findings.why: The question asks about buying "without paying New York sales tax", and this filer did pay New York tax. The help widens the question only to purchases taxed below New York City's rate, so a higher-rate locality outside New York City is missed. The liability can still be charged from the chart and prorated for a part-year abode.

findings.situation: A filer outside New York City paid their own county's full local rate, which is below New York City's rate, and answers yes because of the help text.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 18, Line 59: "its rate of tax is higher than the rate of tax originally paid"
findings.why: The help counts any purchase taxed below New York City's rate. The text imposes extra local tax only when the filer's own locality has a higher rate, so this filer owes nothing on this line.

findings.situation: On a joint return, care is paid so the working spouse can work while the filer is a full-time student or is disabled. The computed helper asks only "so you could work or look for work?", so a filer who reads "you" as themselves alone could answer no.
findings.irs_text: ny_it216i p. 1: "The care was provided so you (and your spouse, if you were married) could work or look for work. ... If you or your spouse was a student or disabled, see the lines 6 and 7 instructions on page 5."
findings.why: The gate's stated wording covers the spouse, but the f2441 helper questions it is actually computed from say only "you." A filer who is the student or disabled spouse could truthfully answer no, which zeroes line 64 when the federal credit, and so the New York credit, would apply.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse rather than the filer paid the care expenses. The helper "Did you pay for the care..." could be read as asking only about the filer's own payments.

findings.why: Eligibility depends on the expenses of the joint filing unit. A helper phrased only as "you" lets a filer answer no when only the spouse paid.

findings.why: The gate is computed from a federal answer, and contributions have no federal consequence. A contributor-only owner could reasonably leave the count at zero and lose the New York contribution deduction.

findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "During 2025, did you, as an account owner, make contributions to or a withdrawal from..."
findings.why: "Had" an account and "own" an account can be read as asking about the present or year-end, while the text reaches any activity during 2025.

findings.situation: A renter pays $480 a month for a furnished apartment, $50 of it for furnishings, so adjusted rent is $430, and owns no real estate.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: "The average monthly rent ... paid was $450 or less, not counting charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, or board."; p. 2 Line 12: "Adjusted rent is the rent paid after subtracting any charges for heat, gas, electricity, furnishings, and board."
findings.why: The question removes heat, gas, electricity and meals but not furnishings, so this filer can truthfully say their rent was over $450. A non-owner may also answer no to the property part, which drops a credit the text allows.

findings.situation: A subsidized tenant's contract rent is $900 a month but the tenant pays $300, and the tenant owns no real estate.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 2 Line 11: "Enter the total rent you or your spouse ... paid during 2025; do not include any subsidized part of your rental charge."; p. 1: "The average monthly rent you or your spouse ... paid was $450 or less"
findings.why: "Was your rent $450 a month or less" can be read as the full contract rent, so the filer answers no even though the rent they paid qualifies.

findings.situation: A renter who owns no real property reads "is all the real estate you own worth $85,000 or less?"
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1: "The current market value of all real property you owned, such as houses, garages, and land, was $85,000 or less."
findings.why: Someone who owns nothing can read this part as not applying and answer no, or as a $0 value and answer yes. Because the question joins two different tests with "or", it is unclear which answer a non-owner should give.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse paid the rent or property taxes, or owns the real estate.

findings.situation: A full-year resident with federal AGI of $18,000 or less who is not a dependent, but who lived in the same New York home for less than six months or whose home was fully exempt from property tax.

findings.situation: A filer moves from New Jersey to Buffalo on January 1, 2025, is a full-year New York State resident for 2025, and has accrued income, but never lives in New York City.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "Full-year New York State residents ... You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 and • you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or • you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026."
findings.why: The State-level trigger is a move into or out of New York State. The computed condition only tests moves into or out of New York City, so it is false for a filer outside the City who is still subject to the special accrual rules.

findings.situation: A full-year resident of Albany moves to another state on January 1, 2026, and has a 2025 bonus that is paid and federally reported in 2026.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026" and "income that was fixed and determinable in tax year 2025, but you will be reporting that income for federal income tax purposes in a tax year after 2025"

findings.situation: A full-year New York State resident moves into or out of New York City partway through 2025, making them a New York City part-year resident, and has income fixed in one City period but reportable in the other.

question:
Did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) make a withdrawal during 2025 from an account under New York's 529 college savings program that is nonqualified for New York?

A withdrawal is nonqualified for New York unless it was used:
- for the beneficiary's qualified higher education expenses at an eligible college or other post-secondary institution
- for the beneficiary's qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses at an eligible educational institution, on or after July 4, 2025
- to pay principal or interest on a qualified education loan of the beneficiary or the beneficiary's sibling
- for a rollover to a Roth IRA or to an ABLE account
- for any purpose, if the withdrawal is the result of the beneficiary's death or disability

Answer Yes for a withdrawal used for elementary or secondary school tuition, or for a transfer to another state's 529 program: New York treats these as nonqualified although they are qualified federally. A transfer between family members' accounts within New York's program, not paid out, is not a withdrawal.

findings.situation: A filer who paid work-related care for a qualifying person but had no federal income tax liability (so the nonrefundable federal credit came to $0 or could not be used) may truthfully read 'would you qualify to claim' as asking whether they could get the federal credit and answer NO, even though the refundable New York credit would be nonzero.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 19, Line 64: "Would you qualify to claim the federal child and dependent care credit for 2025 (whether or not you actually claimed it)? • If No, you do not qualify for this credit."
findings.why: The question covers not claiming the federal credit, but not having been able to benefit from it because of zero federal tax. Because line 64 is a refundable credit, a filer who reads 'qualify' as 'would get an amount' answers NO, and the tool then enters $0 where Form IT-216 would allow a credit.

findings.situation: A filer whose only government-plan income is periodic distributions from a New York State or local government IRC § 457 deferred compensation plan would read it as a distribution from a government plan and answer YES. Line 26 is correctly $0 for these payments.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "You may not subtract the following: ... Periodic distributions from government (IRC § 457) deferred compensation plans."
findings.why: The question asks about any "pension or other distribution ... from a New York State or local government pension plan" and does not exclude 457 plans. So it refuses a case where the tool's line 26 value of $0 is correct.

findings.situation: A filer receiving a TIAA annuity attributable to employment at a private university, or a payment from a supplemental annuity plan funded by salary reduction, could answer YES. The question names TIAA as an example and counts any distribution from the plan, but line 26 is $0 for these amounts.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "You may not subtract ... findings.why: The question's example "(for example an annuity paid by TIAA)" and its plan-based wording make non-qualifying TIAA or supplemental annuity recipients answer YES, even though the tool's $0 is correct for them.

findings.situation: A filer receiving a pension as an employee of a U.S. possession, a political subdivision of a territory or possession, a federal agency or instrumentality, or a public authority other than the three named may not know whether that counts.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 26: "Certain public authorities, including: ..." and "The United States, its territories, possessions (or political subdivisions thereof), or any agency or instrumentality of the United States (including the military)"
findings.why: The question lists only "a U.S. territory or the District of Columbia" and three named authorities. A filer whose employer is a possession, a subdivision, an instrumentality or another public authority could reasonably read the list as closed and answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer has $30,000 of net earnings from self-employment allocated to Zone 1 and $30,000 allocated to Zone 2. Neither zone exceeds $50,000, so no MCTMT is due and the tool's $0 entries are correct. The filer could still read the question as asking about the combined amount and answer YES.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "If an individual's net earnings from self-employment allocated to either zone exceed $50,000 for the tax year, then you are subject to the MCTMT." Also: "Only enter an amount on line 54a if your net earnings from self-employment allocated to Zone 1 exceed $50,000 ... Only enter an amount on line 54b if your net earnings from self-employment allocated to Zone 2 exceed $50,000."
findings.why: The question asks about earnings "allocated to New York City (MCTD Zone 1) or to Zone 2 of more than $50,000". It does not say the $50,000 test applies to each zone separately. A filer can read it as Zone 1 plus Zone 2 combined and answer YES, which refuses a return the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer has more than $50,000 of net earnings from self-employment allocated to a business in Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester, Rockland, Orange, Putnam or Dutchess County. The filer could answer NO because they do not know that "Zone 2" means those counties.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "Zone 2 includes the counties of: – Dutchess – Nassau – Orange – Putnam – Rockland – Suffolk – Westchester"
findings.why: The question names New York City for Zone 1 but leaves "Zone 2" undefined. A filer who does not know the MCTD zones can reasonably answer NO even though the lines require a Zone 2 base, and line 54b would then wrongly be $0.

findings.situation: A partner or S corporation shareholder whose entity reports the partner's share of other states' bond interest (modification EA-113) may truthfully answer NO, because they did not hold the bonds or a fund themselves, yet that amount belongs on line 20.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 7: "If you have either of the addition or subtraction modifications in the chart below, relating to your partnership or S corporation income, include the amount on the corresponding line of Form IT-201. ... EA-113 Interest income on state and local bonds and obligations 20"
findings.why: The question asks only about interest or dividends from bonds, or from tax-exempt mutual or money market funds. It does not mention bond interest passed through from a partnership or S corporation, so a partner can read it as not covering their K-1 share and answer NO, leaving line 20 at $0.

(QDRO) ... • Distributions you received as a result of an annuity contract purchased with your own funds from an insurance company'; also 'but not payments derived from contributions made after you retired'

findings.situation: A filer who turned 59 1/2 during 2025 and received all of their pension, annuity or IRA income before that date must answer YES ('59 1/2 or older in 2025'), although the qualifying amount, and therefore line 29, is $0.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: 'If you became 59½ during 2025, enter only the amount you received after you became 59½'
findings.why: The question tests the person's age during 2025, not whether the income was received after the person reached 59 1/2. It therefore captures filers whose exclusion is zero.

findings.situation: A filer whose federal AGI is $18,000 or less, who lived in the same New York home for six months and paid rent or property tax, but whose home's market value or average monthly rent exceeds the Form IT-214 limits, would answer YES even though the credit is zero.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 19, Line 67: "Review the instructions for Form IT-214, Claim for Real Property Tax Credit for Homeowners and Renters, to see if you qualify for this credit."
findings.why: The help lists only the income, six-month residence and payment tests. It omits Form IT-214's other limits, such as the property market value cap and the average monthly rent cap. A filer who meets the listed tests answers YES to "Might you qualify", but the correct line 67 amount is 0, which the tool already computes.

findings.situation: A filer whose own federal AGI is $18,000 or less but whose household gross income (other household members plus nontaxable income) exceeds $18,000 cannot tell from the help which income the limit tests.
findings.irs_text: ny_it214i p. 1, Do I qualify for this credit?: "Your federal adjusted gross income was $18,000 or less." (Form IT-214 also applies a household gross income test.)
findings.why: The help says "income of $18,000 or less" without saying whose income or which measure. A filer could read it as their own AGI and answer YES (wide), or as household income and answer NO. The question's "if unsure, read the Form IT-214 instructions" softens this but does not settle it.

findings.situation: A filer who moved into New York City on January 1, 2025 from elsewhere in New York State has New York-source income, such as a bonus from a New York employer, that became fixed and determinable in 2024 and is reported federally in 2025.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "You have accrued income for 2025 if you have an item of: • non-New York source income that was fixed and determinable in a tax year prior to 2025, but you are reporting that income for federal income tax purposes in tax year 2025"; "*Non-New York source income is income that is not attributable to: • a business, trade, profession, or occupation carried on in New York State, or • the ownership of any interest in real or tangible personal property in New York State."
findings.why: The question asks about any "income fixed and determinable in one tax year but reported federally in another". This filer must answer YES and is refused. Under the text, prior-year New York-source income is not accrued income, so the filer is not subject to the special accrual rules and the tool computes line 1 correctly.

findings.situation: A filer who moved into or out of New York City at the year boundary has income that was fixed in one year and reported in another, but neither year is 2025 (for example, fixed in 2023 and reported in 2024).
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "income that was fixed and determinable in tax year 2025, but you will be reporting that income for federal income tax purposes in a tax year after 2025" and "fixed and determinable in a tax year prior to 2025, but you are reporting that income ... in tax year 2025"
findings.why: The question says only "one tax year ... another" and never ties either year to 2025. A filer could read it as covering any timing difference and answer YES, or as covering only 2025 accruals and answer NO. Only accruals that involve 2025 count under the text.

findings.situation: A filer received dividends from a mutual fund that invests in U.S. government obligations but does not meet the 50% asset requirement each quarter, so nothing is subtractable and line 28 is correctly $0, yet the question makes the filer answer YES.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: "Dividends you received from a regulated investment company (mutual fund) that invests in obligations of the U.S. government and meet the 50% asset requirement each quarter qualify for this subtraction." Question: "or dividends from a fund investing in them, in federal income?"
findings.why: The question covers any fund that invests in U.S. obligations, with no 50% quarterly asset test. A non-qualifying fund's dividends give a $0 subtraction, which the tool computes correctly, but the filer is still refused.

findings.situation: A filer's Schedule K-1 from a partnership, S corporation, estate or trust passes through interest on U.S. government obligations held by the entity, reported on line 11, and the filer truthfully answers NO because the bonds are not "your" bonds.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: "Did you include interest income from U.S. government bonds or other U.S. government obligations on lines 2, 6, or 11? ... If Yes, enter the amount of interest income you earned from bonds or other obligations of the U.S. government."
findings.why: The NY text covers any such interest included on line 11, with no requirement that the filer own the bonds. The question asks about interest from "your" bonds, so pass-through interest from entity-held obligations can be missed, and the tool then enters $0.

findings.situation: A filer whose qualifying fund dividends are only partly derived from federal obligations, or who cannot tell whether the fund meets the 50% test, cannot tell whether "dividends from a fund investing in them" means any such fund or only a qualifying one.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: "The portion of the qualifying dividends that may be subtracted is based upon the portion of the taxable income received by the mutual fund that is derived from federal obligations. Contact the mutual fund for additional information on meeting the 50% asset requirement"
findings.why: "A fund investing in them" could mean a fund holding any U.S. obligations or only a fund that qualifies. The help text mentions only 1099-INT box 3 and gives no guidance on fund dividends.
